summary: From a boat, Jesus tells the parable of the sower, then explains to His disciples why He speaks in parables and what the four kinds of ground mean.
key_insight: Every kind of ground receives the seed, and even on the stony and thorny ground it springs up. The difference is not whether people hear the word but what happens after they hear it. Luke says the good ground keeps it and bears fruit “with patience.”
story: On the same day, Jesus went out of the house and sat by the sea. {Mt} A great crowd gathered, people coming to Him from every city, {Lk} so He got into a boat and sat in it on the sea, while the whole multitude stood on the shore facing Him. Then He taught them many things by parables. {Mk}

“Listen! Behold, a sower went out to sow.” {Mk} Some seed fell by the wayside, where it was trampled down {Lk} and the birds devoured it. Some fell on stony ground with little earth; it sprang up quickly, but when the sun rose it was scorched and withered, because it had no root. Some fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up and choked it. But other seed fell on good ground and yielded a crop, some a hundredfold, some sixty, some thirty. {Mt} Then Jesus cried out, “He who has ears to hear, let him hear!” {Lk}

Later, when He was alone, the Twelve and others around Him asked about the parable. {Mk} “Why do You speak to them in parables?” {Mt} He answered, “Because it has been given to you to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, but to them it has not been given.” In the crowd, Isaiah’s prophecy was coming true: they saw without seeing and heard without understanding, for their hearts had grown dull and they had closed their eyes. But to the disciples He said, “Blessed are your eyes for they see, and your ears for they hear.” {Mt}

“Do you not understand this parable? How then will you understand all the parables?” {Mk} Then He explained it. “The seed is the word of God.” {Lk} The seed by the wayside is the hearer from whom the devil takes away the word, “lest they should believe and be saved.” {Lk} The stony ground is the one who receives the word with joy but has no root, and stumbles when tribulation or persecution comes because of the word. The thorny ground is the one in whom the cares of this world, the deceitfulness of riches and the desires for other things choke the word, so it becomes unfruitful. {Mk}

The good ground is the one who hears the word and understands it, {Mt} who keeps it with “a noble and good heart” and bears fruit with patience, {Lk} some thirtyfold, some sixty, and some a hundred. {Mk}

No one lights a lamp and hides it under a vessel or a bed, Jesus said; he sets it on a lampstand. Nothing hidden will stay hidden. “Therefore take heed how you hear. For whoever has, to him more will be given; and whoever does not have, even what he seems to have will be taken from him.” {Lk}
differences: Matthew lists the yields as a hundredfold, sixty and thirty; Mark gives them in rising order, thirty, sixty and a hundred; Luke mentions only a hundredfold.
Matthew says Jesus speaks in parables “because seeing they do not see.” Mark and Luke introduce Isaiah’s words with “so that” and “that.”
Matthew alone quotes Isaiah 6 in full and adds the blessing on the disciples’ eyes and ears. Mark alone records Jesus asking, “Do you not understand this parable?”

Luke alone says the wayside seed was trampled and calls the seed “the word of God.” Luke follows the explanation at once with the lamp and the warning, “take heed how you hear”; Mark gives similar sayings just after his account (Mark 4:21–25).

fit.question: Matthew says Jesus speaks in parables “because” the people do not see. Mark says He does it “so that” they may not see. Did Jesus use parables to explain or to hide?

points.label: Both at once
points.text: Parables open the truth to those who come asking, as the disciples did, and leave it closed to those who have already refused it. The same story reveals to one listener and conceals from another.

points.label: Hardening follows refusal
points.text: Matthew’s fuller quotation of Isaiah 6 shows the order: “their eyes they have closed.” Mark’s “so that” describes God’s judgment on people who had already shut their eyes, the same pattern as in Isaiah’s day.

points.label: A door left open
points.text: In the same breath Jesus says that nothing hidden will stay hidden (Luke 8:17) and calls everyone with ears to hear. The parables are a judgment and an invitation together.

fit.note: Matthew stresses the cause and Mark the result; together they show God’s judgment answering human refusal, with the invitation still open.
fit.short: Parables reveal to the willing and conceal from the hardened. Matthew stresses the cause, the people’s closed eyes; Mark stresses the result.

scene.label: A boat for a pulpit
scene.text: A curved bay between Capernaum and Tabgha, often called the Cove of the Sower, rises from the water like a natural theater. No one can prove this was the spot, but it shows how a voice from a boat could carry to thousands on the slope.

scene.label: Sowing by hand
scene.text: A farmer scattered seed by hand as he walked, so some landed on the hard paths that ran through and around the fields. In many fields, rock lies just under a thin layer of soil, where seed sprouts fast in the warmth and dies as fast in the sun.

scene.label: Thorns
scene.text: Thistles and thornbushes spring up quickly in Galilee’s fields. They take the water and light that young grain needs and soon overshadow it.

scene.label: A hundredfold
scene.text: When Isaac reaped a hundredfold, Scripture adds that “the LORD blessed him” (Genesis 26:12). Ordinary harvests were far smaller. Thirty, sixty and a hundred would have sounded like extraordinary abundance.

scene.label: “Mysteries”
scene.text: In the New Testament a mystery is not a riddle. It is something God kept hidden and now makes known (Romans 16:25–26). Jesus gives it to those who come to Him asking.

witnesses.matthew: Opens the third of the five great teaching sections of his Gospel with this parable (chapter 13). He quotes Isaiah 6 in full to show that Israel’s dull hearing fulfills Scripture, and he adds that prophets and righteous men longed to see what the disciples saw.
witnesses.mark: Presents the sower as the key to all the parables: “How then will you understand all the parables?” Mark begins with the command “Listen!” and lets the yields climb from thirty to sixty to a hundred.
witnesses.luke: Calls the seed “the word of God” and describes the good ground as “a noble and good heart” that keeps the word. Luke ends with the lamp and the warning “take heed how you hear,” then moves straight to Jesus’ true family.

seeing.reveals: Jesus speaks the word of the kingdom, and He scatters it generously on every kind of ground. He is confident that His word will bear fruit far beyond what anyone could expect, even when much of it seems wasted.
seeing.living: Every hearer meets the same seed. What differs is the ground: a heart hardened like a footpath, a joy with no roots, a life choked by worry and money, or a heart that hears, holds on and waits patiently for fruit. Jesus’ warning is personal: “take heed how you hear.”
seeing.ponder: Which kind of ground best describes how you have received Jesus’ word this past month, and what is crowding it out?

preaching.big_idea: The same seed falls on every heart; how we hear decides what grows.
outline: The warning: take heed how you hear (16–18)
preaching.watch_for: The passage is framed by calls to listen: “He who has ears to hear, let him hear!” (v. 8) and “take heed how you hear” (v. 18). It is a parable about hearing, told to hearers.
